title: DOJ open to exemptions to abortion as a crime amid drafting of criminal code

blocks.text: Justice Undersecretary Raul Vasquez said the Department of Justice (DOJ) maintains that abortion is a crime but added that the DOJ was open to proposing exemptions with proposed amendments to the Revised Penal Code (RPC) pending before the House of Representatives.
At a news briefing, Vasquez said that a DOJ committee has prepared a draft Criminal Code of the Philippines which aims to amend the RPC.
Asked about several laws that could change with the code, Vasquez said there has been an effort by some progressive lawmakers to decriminalize abortion.
“Our position in the DOJ is that abortion is okay as a crime still because of the constitutional mandate. At the same time, our culture still prohibits such conduct,” Vasquez said.

“We are also open to the possibility of giving exemptions like for therapeutic purposes or… I have even instructed our prosecutors or committee members who are attending there actively under my guidance, I have asked them also to be open to the possibility of allowing that in, for instance, rape,” he added.
Other matters being discussed was the topic of adultery and concubinage.

Under Philippine law, adultery is committed by a married woman who had sexual intercourse with a man, while concubinage is when a married man keeps a mistress under certain circumstances, including having intercourse with her and cohabiting a place with her.

“That is one of the major reforms we initiated because there really is a huge divide between adultery and concubinage. So the proposal is to make it equal… I would say that it is quite controversial, even in the discussion before the House of Representatives, because there is a resistance to do it in the same way,” Vasquez said.

“Adultery is committed by a single act of sexual misconduct committed by a married woman, on the other hand, concubinage requires certain circumstances or factors to be considered before they could be prosecuted,” he added.
Other laws being considered for revision included laws on espionage and libel, according to the DOJ executive. —NB, GMA News
